claims.claim: Puberty is the body's natural process of sexual maturation — the time in life when a person's body becomes sexually mature.

The hormonal trigger of puberty begins in the brain: the hypothalamus secretes gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which stimulates the pituitary gland to release LH and FSH, which signal the ovaries and testes to release estrogens and testosterone — the hormones that launch the other signs of puberty. This brain-to-sex-gland chain is named the HPG (hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal) axis in the lesson.

The physical changes of puberty include a growth spurt (a rapid increase in height lasting roughly two to three years, bringing young people closer to adult height), body changes (body hair, acne, deepening voice, and changes in muscle and fat distribution), and reproductive maturity (maturation of the sex organs; menarche usually around ages 12-13 and spermarche around 13-14).

Puberty typically begins between ages 8 and 13 for girls and between ages 9 and 14 for boys; the onset and pace of puberty vary widely, and NICHD defines precocious (abnormally early) and delayed (abnormally late) puberty relative to these ranges while noting that many children with only slightly early onset experience no major psychological or social problems.

The same hormones that drive the physical changes of puberty also drive brain development in adolescence; adolescents experience a phase shift in the sleep-wake cycle (documented by Mary Carskadon and colleagues) that is tied to pubertal changes in melatonin secretion, so later bedtimes and wake times are typical — and mood shifts during this period are a normal part of the process.

Societies frame the transition into adulthood differently — cultural expectations shape how the changes of puberty are understood and responded to, and the timing of puberty varies from person to person and from country to country.
Puberty is a normal developmental transition: it transforms a child's body into an adult body as part of the ordinary course of human development, not a problem to be solved.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The age range for the start of puberty differs across sources and countries.
positions: NICHD and MedlinePlus: typically between ages 8 and 13 for girls and 9 and 14 for boys (current U.S. clinical convention).
Britannica (2015): 'usually occurs between ages 11 and 16,' with variation by country and population.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the NICHD/MedlinePlus ranges as the primary statement (stated as typical ranges, not deadlines) and incorporates Britannica's point that timing varies across countries and populations as a supporting line.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether early pubertal timing causes psychological or social problems.
positions: Some research (cited in OpenStax) links early timing to psychological difficulty in some adolescents.
NICHD: many children with only slightly early onset experience no major psychological or social problems.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the honest note — early and late timing both matter, and within the typical range both are usually normal — without claiming inevitable harm and without clinical advice (clinical care is out of scope).

unsupportedExistingClaims: No machine-generated draft was consulted for this topic; the lesson was written from the task scope and verified sources only.
correctionsNeeded: Kept the growth spurt description to MedlinePlus's 'rapid increase in height lasting about two to three years' rather than giving a fixed inch-per-year figure.
Attributed the sleep-phase shift to Mary Carskadon and colleagues per OpenStax Lifespan Development rather than presenting it as generic knowledge.
Framed precocious and delayed puberty strictly as NICHD definitions of the extremes, with an explicit note that slightly early or late timing is usually normal variation.
rightsIssues: All sources used reference-only; NICHD and MedlinePlus content is U.S. government public-domain material, and OpenStax texts are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — in both cases facts were synthesized into original prose and no source wording was reproduced at length.
Britannica is a licensed reference source; it was used for background confirmation of one general claim only, with no prose adapted.
No new source ids conflict with existing registries; a registry-wide search for 'puberty' returned no prior records, so all seven ids are new mints.
